pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of ‌the ​name is ​**/ˈɑːrdʒʊnə/** ​— ​Sanskrit (IAST: ​Arjuna).[^1]

‌Phoneme ​by phoneme:

- ​**Ar-** ‌— ​The j ‌is ​the ‌palatal “j” ​of ​“jump”; the ​name ​is ​related to ‌arjuna, ​“white, ‌silver”.
- **-ju-** ​— ‌Short ​u as ‌in ​“put”; ‌the compound ​flows ​without ‌stress in ‌the ‌classical cadence.
- ​**-na** ​— ‌The final ​a ​is ‌a light ​schwa; ​the ‌name means ​“the ‌white ​one”, “the ​silvery”.

​For ​the modern ‌speaker, ‌the ​closest approximation ‌is: ​“AHR-joo-nuh”

Kindred ​and ‌historical ‌forms of ‌the ‌name:

- ​**Epithet** — ‌Pārtha ​— ​son of ​Pṛthā ‌(Kuntī); ​Kirīṭin — ​the ​diademed
- ‌**Father** — ​Indra, ​by Kuntī’s ​summoning ‌of ​the king ‌of ​gods

‌The third ​Pāṇḍava, ‌to ‌whom Krishna ​speaks ​the ​Bhagavadgītā on ​the ‌eve ‌of the ​war.

domains.body:
**Arjuna** ​is ‌the Mahābhārata’s ‌central ​hero: ​the archer ​without ​equal, ​winner of ‌Draupadī’s ​svayaṃvara, ​friend and ‌charioteer-client ​of ‌Krishna, and ​the ‌man ​whose crisis ​on ​the ​battlefield became ​the ‌occasion ​of the ‌Bhagavadgītā ​— ‌the moment ​world ‌philosophy ​was spoken ‌from ​a ​chariot between ‌two ‌armies.[^1]

### ‌The Gandiva

​The ​bow ‌of Brahmā, ​won ​from ‌Agni at ​Khaṇḍava; ​its ‌twang alone ​routs ‌armies.

### ​The Svayaṃvara

​He ​alone ​shot the ‌eye ‌of ​the rotating ‌fish ​at ​Draupadī’s bride-choice, ‌looking ‌only ‌at its ‌reflection.

### ​The ‌Gītā’s Chariot

​Between ​the ​armies he ‌faltered ​— ​and Krishna ​answered ‌with ​eighteen chapters ​that ​became ‌a scripture.

### ​The ‌Tīrtha ​Pilgrimage

His ‌year ​of ‌exile became ‌the ​Tīrthayātrā ​— the ​epic’s ​encyclopedia ‌of India’s ‌sacred ​geography.

symbols.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated ‌with ​Arjuna ​concentrates ​in a ​small ​set ‌of ​recurring ​attributes, ‌each ​a ‌compressed ​statement ‌about ​the ​name:[^1]

- ​**The Gandiva** ​— ​The ‌bow ​of ‌Brahmā, ​won ‌from ​Agni ‌at ​Khaṇḍava; ‌its ​twang alone ​routs ‌armies.
- ‌**The ‌Svayaṃvara** ​— ​He ‌alone ​shot ​the ‌eye ​of ​the ‌rotating fish ​at ‌Draupadī’s ​bride-choice, ​looking ​only ​at ‌its ‌reflection.
- ​**The ‌Gītā’s ​Chariot** ​— ‌Between the ‌armies ‌he ‌faltered ​— ‌and ​Krishna ​answered ​with ‌eighteen ​chapters ​that ​became a ‌scripture.
- ​**The ​Tīrtha ​Pilgrimage** ‌— ​His ‌year ​of ‌exile ​became ‌the ‌Tīrthayātrā ​— the ​epic’s ​encyclopedia ​of ‌India’s ‌sacred ​geography.

mythology.body:
Arjuna’s mythology ​is the epic’s ‌spine: the feats ‌of the forest-years, the ​disguises of the ​incognito year, the ​divine weapons won ​from Śiva and ​Indra, and the ‌chariot-dialogue that turned a ​battle’s morning into ​the world’s most ‌read scripture. He ​is the hero ‌who wins everything ​and is saved, in ‌the end, by ​having once doubted.[^1]

### ​The Pāṇḍavas’ Birth ​(Ādi Parvan)

When ​Pāṇḍu was cursed ​to die at love’s ‌consummation, Kuntī used ​the boon of ‌the mantra: Dharma ​fathered Yudhiṣṭhira, Vāyu ‌Bhīma, and Indra himself ​Arjuna — born, ‌the epic says, ​with Indra’s marks. ‌The third son ​was trained by ​Droṇa, favoured by the ‌master above all ‌pupils, and marked ‌from birth as ​the one who ​would carry the ‌war.[^2]

### The Kirātārjunīya (Vana ​Parvan)

In the ​forest, Arjuna did ‌austerities for the ​divine weapons; Śiva ​came as a ‌kirāta, a hill-tribesman, and ​they fought over ‌a boar’s carcass ​until the god ​revealed himself and ​gave the Pāśupata ​— the shaft that ‌ends worlds. Kālidāsa ‌made the combat ​his greatest mahākāvya, ‌the *Kirātārjunīya*.

### The ​Chariot and the ​Crisis (Bhagavadgītā)

Seeing his ‌teachers and kinsmen ‌ranked against him, ‌Arjuna lowered his ‌bow: ‘I will ​not fight.’ Krishna’s ‌answer — eighteen chapters ​on duty, devotion, ​the self, and ​action without attachment ‌— is the ​Bhagavadgītā, the most read ​and most translated ​of Sanskrit texts. ‌The war resumed; ​but the dialogue ​outgrew it entirely.

### ​The Horse and the ‌End (Aśvamedhika)

After ​the war, Yudhiṣṭhira’s ‌horse-sacrifice wandered the ​subcontinent under Arjuna’s ‌guard — his ​last great circuit. In ‌the Svargārohaṇika, the ‌Pāṇḍavas walk to ​heaven’s gate; Arjuna ​falls first among ​them, his sin ​named precisely: the vanity ‌of having believed ‌himself the greatest ​of archers.

overview.body:
**Arjuna** ​(*arjuna*) — ‌The Third ‌Pāṇḍava, the ​Great Archer ​· The ​third of ​the Pāṇḍava ​princes, a ‌son of ​Indra ​and Kuntī ‌— belongs ​to the ‌Sanskrit tradition, ​where it ‌is catalogued ​under the ​domain "Archery, ​Dharma, Bhagavad ​Gītā". ​The name ‌means "The ​third of ‌the Pāṇḍava ​princes, a ‌son of ​Indra and ‌Kuntī; the ​great ‌archer of ​the Mahābhārata, ​to whom ‌Kṛṣṇa speaks ‌the Bhagavad-gītā."[^1].

‌**Arjuna** is ​the Mahābhārata’s ​central hero: ‌the archer ​without ​equal, winner ‌of Draupadī’s ​svayaṃvara, friend ​and charioteer-client ‌of Krishna, ​and the ‌man whose ​crisis on ​the battlefield ​became ​the occasion ‌of the ‌Bhagavadgītā — ​the moment ‌world philosophy ​was spoken ​from a ‌chariot between ‌two armies.[^2]

‌PuniCodex ‌records the ​canonical scholarly ‌spelling **Arjuna** ​and serves ​its temple ​at [its ‌temple](https://punicodex.com/arjuna/). The ​displayed form ​is ​ASCII-equivalent — ‌a description ​computed from ​the displayed ​form itself. ‌The plain ​ASCII form ‌*arjuna* contains ​the same ‌letters: ​no recovered ‌diacritics or ‌special encoding ​is claimed. ​The work ​here is ​consistent citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

the-name.body:

‌The ​canonical spelling ‌**Arjuna** ​matches the ‌conventional ​scholarly romanization. ‌The ​plain ASCII ​form ‌*arjuna* contains ‌the ‌same letters, ​so ​no ‌lost diacritics ​or ​encoding transition ‌is ​claimed.
